<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README, this project is the ffuf tool – a fast web fuzzer written in Go. Its core purpose is to perform different kinds of HTTP fuzzing (e.g., directory discovery, vhost discovery, parameter fuzzing, POST data fuzzing) by varying parts of the URL, headers, or request parameters using the FUZZ keyword. The project’s design combines several distinct functional areas that work together to create a highly configurable fuzzing engine with support for features such as autocalibration, interactive filtering, multiple modes of input, output handling (in various formats), and even integration with external mutators.

Below is a guideline on how to draw the most accurate and detailed system architecture diagram for this project:

1. Main Components:
   • Client/CLI Entry Point: Represented by main.go and help.go. This is where the command-line arguments are parsed and jobs are initiated.
   • Core Engine (Fuzzing & Runner): The “pkg/ffuf” package contains core fuzzing logic, configuration parsing, options handling, job creation, request/response handling, progress tracking, and error management.
   • Input Management: The “pkg/input” package handles loading and parsing wordlists, processing FUZZ keywords, and possibly handling external input (via --input-cmd).
   • Filtering: The “pkg/filter” package deals with applying matchers and filters (e.g., filtering based on HTTP status codes, word count, response size, etc.) to the responses.
   • Output Management: The “pkg/output” package is responsible for formatting and writing the results (e.g., to JSON, HTML, CSV, Markdown, and writing to files or stdout).
   • Request Runner: The “pkg/runner” package (with subtypes like simple runner) orchestrates how HTTP requests are scheduled and executed concurrently over multiple threads.
   • Scraping: The “pkg/scraper” package is used for extracting or further processing fetched response payloads.
   • Interactive Mode: The “pkg/interactive” package handles the interactive shell that enables pausing, filter reconfiguration, and job management mid-execution.
   • Utilities: Various utility functions are shared among packages (e.g., in pkg/ffuf/util.go, pkg/ffuf/multierror.go).

2. Relationships and Interactions:
   • The CLI layer (main.go) reads user input and options, then creates a configuration object that is consumed by the core engine.
   • The core engine delegates input handling to the Input Manager which prepares the list of fuzzing targets.
   • The Runner component loops over the inputs (or "jobs"), creating and dispatching HTTP requests.
   • Each request goes through the Filtering module where responses are screened using matchers defined by the user.
   • Valid results are sent to the Output Manager for formatted display and saving to files.
   • The interactive component can take over to allow dynamic reconfiguration, affecting filtering or runner state.
   • Utilities support error management, constants, and configuration marshalling across modules.
   
3. Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   • Modular design with separation of concerns – distinct packages perform dedicated tasks.
   • Extension / plug-in friendly: Input, filtering, and formatting can be extended or integrated with external tools (e.g., external mutators).
   • Concurrency: The runner is explicitly designed to handle concurrent HTTP requests.
   • Command line application patterns: The project uses flags and configuration file inheritance (with ffufrc) as well as an interactive shell for runtime control.

4. Relevant Frameworks and Dependencies:
   • Written entirely in Go (modules: go.mod & go.sum) and relies on Go’s concurrency primitives.
   • Integration with GitHub Actions for continuous integration (as seen in the .github/workflows directory).
   • Uses GoReleaser (in .goreleaser.yml) for release creation.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram to ffuf:
   - Clearly separate the main CLI/entry point from the core processing libraries.
   - Depict the flow from command-line input → configuration parsing → input loading → job runner → HTTP request generation → filtering → output management.
   - Include a node for “Interactive Mode” that hooks into or overrides the main fuzzing loop.
   - Use directional arrows to indicate data and control flows (e.g., from Input to Runner, from Runner to Filter, and from Filter to Output).
   - Use distinct shapes or color coding to differentiate between internal packages (core engine, filtering, input/output) versus external dependencies (HTTP endpoints, external mutator commands).
   - Mark the concurrency aspect by showing multiple “request worker” threads/processes under the Runner module.

6. Diagram Elements to Include:
   - Boxes labeled “CLI/Entry Point” (main.go, help.go)
   - A central box for “Core Engine” (pkg/ffuf) that connects to submodules.
   - Separate, clearly labeled boxes for “Input Management”, “Filter Module”, “Runner”, “Output Management”, “Interactive Shell”, and “Scraper”.
   - Arrows showing the flow:
       • From CLI to Input Management (fetching wordlists and parameters).
       • From Input Manager to Runner (job scheduling).
       • From Runner to Filter (response evaluation).
       • From Filter to Output Management (results presentation).
       • A feedback arrow from Interactive Shell to Runner/Filter indicating runtime reconfiguration.
   - Annotation for concurrency (e.g., “40 concurrent threads” can be shown as a note in the Runner box).
   - A side note indicating that configuration files (ffufrc, command-line flags) affect the operation globally.

7. Final Instruction for Detailed Diagram:
   - Ensure all components are clearly labeled with their respective package names or file groupings.
   - Use directional arrows to indicate how HTTP request data moves from configuration through processing to output.
   - Include legends for color coding, for example:
         • Blue boxes for CLI and external configurations,
         • Green boxes for runtime components (input, filtering, running),
         • Orange boxes for post-processing and output.
   - Annotate any external dependencies (external mutator, target web servers, etc.) that illustrate points of integration.

This detailed breakdown should help you, as a principal software engineer, to map the entire structure and data flows of ffuf in a comprehensive system architecture diagram tailored exactly to its functionality and design principles.
